slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on special purpose books. A business with hundreds of transactions cannot record them all in a single journal. So it keeps separate books for cash, small payments, purchases, sales and returns, and a journal proper for everything else. In this part we study the cash book with a bank column and the petty cash book, using imagined firms.

slides.heading: Why special purpose books
slides.body_md: Each book collects **one kind** of transaction.

rows: Different clerks keep different books at the same time
Each clerk becomes skilled in one kind of entry
Like transactions are together and totals are posted once
A transaction of one kind is found in one book

visual.alt: Table of four advantages of special purpose books: division of work, specialisation, saving of time and easy reference

slides.narration: Special purpose books save effort in four ways. Division of work lets different clerks keep different books. Specialisation makes each clerk skilled in one kind of entry. Time is saved because like transactions are together and their totals can be posted at once. And a transaction is easy to find when it is needed. All of this is hard with one journal.

slides.narration: Every book starts from a source document. Cash memos, cheques and pay in slips go to the cash book. Petty cash vouchers go to the petty cash book. Purchase invoices go to the purchases book and sales invoices to the sales book. Debit notes and credit notes go to the return books. Anything else goes to the journal proper. Totals from these books are then posted to the ledger.

slides.heading: The cash book
slides.body_md: The cash book is a book of **original entry** and also the **cash account** of the ledger. Receipts go on the debit side; payments on the credit side.

rows: Cash and bank receipts and payments
Small payments on the imprest system
Cash: debit or nil. Bank: debit or credit (overdraft)
Debit: the balance of the imprest not yet spent

visual.alt: Table of the simple cash book, the cash book with a bank column and the petty cash book: what each records and what kind of balance it can show

slides.narration: The cash book is both a book of original entry and a ledger account. Receipts go on the debit side and payments on the credit side. A simple cash book has one column for cash, and its balance is always a debit balance or nil. A cash book with a bank column has two money columns, cash and bank. Small payments are kept in a separate petty cash book.

slides.narration: Here is the format of a two column cash book. The debit side holds receipts and the credit side holds payments. slides.narration: A contra entry is a transaction between cash and bank, so both columns are affected and the entry appears on both sides of the same book. When cash is deposited into the bank, the cash column is credited and the bank column is debited. When cash is withdrawn from the bank for office use, the cash column is debited and the bank column is credited. Each line is marked with the letter C.

slides.narration: Petty cash covers small payments such as stamps, fares and tea. Under the imprest system the head cashier gives the petty cashier a fixed amount. The petty cashier pays small expenses against vouchers. At the end of the period the payments are totalled and the balance found. The head cashier then reimburses exactly the amount spent, so the fixed amount is restored.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Special purpose books give division of work, specialisation, saving of time and easy reference.
The cash book is both journal and ledger; cash is never a credit balance.
Contra entries are written on both sides and marked C; an overdraft is a credit balance in the bank column.
Petty cash on the imprest system: reimburse the amount spent.

rows: Division of work, specialisation, saving of time, easy reference

Contra entries marked C; cheques; bank charges; overdraft is a credit balance

visual.alt: Summary table of special purpose books, the cash book, the bank column and the petty cash book

slides.narration: To sum up. Special purpose books divide the work and save time. The cash book is both a journal and a ledger, and its cash column never shows a credit balance. A cash book with a bank column uses contra entries, written on both sides, and shows an overdraft as a credit balance in the bank column. In petty cash on the imprest system, the amount spent is reimbursed, and the float is restored.

bullets: Write each contra entry on both sides and mark it C.
Balance the cash and bank columns separately; a credit cash balance means an error.
In petty cash, make the analysis columns agree with the total column.

rows: Write contra entries on both sides and mark them C
A contra entry written once leaves the columns out of balance
Total and balance each column separately
Cash and bank are balanced independently
Check that the cash balance is a debit
A credit cash balance signals an error
Check analysis columns against the total column
It catches a missed or misplaced voucher

decks.title: Special Purpose Books — Part 2: Purchases, Sales, Returns and Journal Proper
goals: Record credit purchases and sales of goods at the net amount after trade discount, with tax at an imagined rate
Record returns through debit notes and credit notes and post the totals of each book
Pass journal proper entries for opening, rectification, adjustment, drawings, charity, free samples and loss by fire

slides.heading: Purchases, sales and returns books; the journal proper
slides.body_md: Part 2: the books for **credit purchases and sales of goods**, their **returns**, and the **journal proper**.

rows: Ledger folio of the supplier account after posting
Net amount after trade discount (and tax columns when tax is charged)

visual.alt: Table of the format of the purchases book: date, invoice number, name of supplier, ledger folio and amount

slides.narration: In this part we study the books for credit purchases and credit sales of goods, and for goods returned. We see how trade discount and goods and services tax appear in them at an imagined rate. We then study the journal proper, where all the entries that fit no special book are made. All firms and figures are imagined.

slides.heading: The purchases book
slides.body_md: Only **credit purchases of goods**, at the **net amount** after trade discount.

rows: Ledger folio of the supplier account after posting
Net amount after trade discount (and tax columns when tax is charged)

visual.alt: Table of the format of the purchases book: date, invoice number, name of supplier, ledger folio and amount

slides.narration: The purchases book records only credit purchases of goods that the firm deals in. Its format has the date, the invoice number, the name of the supplier, the ledger folio and the amount. Cash purchases go to the cash book, and assets bought on credit go to the journal proper. The ledger folio is filled in after the supplier account has been posted.

slides.heading: Trade discount and the net amount
slides.body_md: Trade discount is deducted on the invoice, so the books show **only the net amount**. Tax is computed on that net amount.

nodes.label: Add tax at the stated rate

visual.alt: Flow from list price to invoice total: list price, less trade discount, net amount recorded in the book, add tax at the rate stated in the problem, invoice total
visual.caption: Only the net amount goes in the goods column.

slides.narration: Trade discount is a reduction in the list price, allowed by the seller at the time of sale. It is deducted on the invoice, so the books record only the net amount. Goods and services tax, at the rate stated in the problem, is computed on that net amount and added to find the invoice total. Discount for early payment is a different thing, called cash discount.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from list price to invoice total
slides.body_md: **Anvi Traders**, July. Tax at an **imagined rate of 12%**. Four invoices; the last is from another state.
bullets: Trade discount: list price × rate.
Tax: net amount × 12 / 100; split equally into CGST and SGST for the same state, or IGST for another state.

visual.alt: Working for the purchases book of Anvi Traders: list prices 1,10,000 rupees, trade discount 16,000, net 94,000, tax 11,280 at an imagined 12 per cent, invoice total 1,05,280 rupees

slides.narration: Anvi Traders received four invoices in July. The list prices total rupees one lakh ten thousand. After trade discount of rupees sixteen thousand, the net amount is rupees ninety four thousand. Tax at an imagined rate of twelve per cent is rupees eleven thousand two hundred eighty, so the invoices total rupees one lakh five thousand two hundred eighty. The last invoice is from another state, so its tax is all integrated tax.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the purchases book
slides.body_md: Only the **net** amounts go in the goods column; tax goes in its own columns.

visual.alt: Purchases book of Anvi Traders for July: net 94,000, CGST 4,020, SGST 4,020, IGST 3,240, total 1,05,280 rupees

slides.narration: The purchases book of Anvi Traders shows each invoice with its net amount and its tax columns. The net amounts total rupees ninety four thousand. Central tax is rupees four thousand twenty, state tax is the same, and integrated tax is rupees three thousand two hundred forty. The invoice total is rupees one lakh five thousand two hundred eighty, which is what the firm owes its suppliers.

slides.heading: Quick check: net amount
slides.body_md: Find the net amount to be entered for an invoice.
slides.narration: Start from the list price. Work out the trade discount at the given per cent and subtract it. The tax does not change the net amount, because tax has its own columns.

slides.heading: Posting the purchases book
slides.body_md: As of 2024, tax paid on purchases is debited to **Input** tax accounts; the rate in each problem is imagined.

rows: *(Being the total of the purchases book posted)*

visual.alt: Posting summary of the purchases book: debit Purchases 94,000, Input CGST 4,020, Input SGST 4,020, Input IGST 3,240; credit the suppliers 1,05,280 rupees in all

slides.narration: At the end of the month the totals of the purchases book are posted. Purchases account is debited with the net total of rupees ninety four thousand. The input tax accounts are debited with the tax. Each supplier is credited with the invoice totals. The debits and the credits both come to rupees one lakh five thousand two hundred eighty. This dated note is as of two thousand twenty four.

slides.heading: The sales book
slides.body_md: Credit **sales of goods** only, at the net amount after trade discount. Tax collected goes to **Output** tax accounts.

visual.alt: Sales book of Anvi Traders for July: net 1,30,500, CGST 4,590, SGST 4,590, IGST 6,480, total 1,46,160 rupees

slides.narration: The sales book is the mirror of the purchases book. It records credit sales of goods in which the firm deals, at the net amount after trade discount, with tax columns. Anvi Traders had four sales in July. The net amounts total rupees one lakh thirty thousand five hundred, central tax is rupees four thousand five hundred ninety, integrated tax is rupees six thousand four hundred eighty, and the customers owe rupees one lakh forty six thousand one hundred sixty.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: posting the sales book
slides.body_md: Customers are **debited**; Sales and the Output tax accounts are **credited**.

rows: *(Being the total of the sales book posted)*

visual.alt: Posting summary of the sales book: debit the customers 1,46,160 rupees; credit Sales 1,30,500, Output CGST 4,590, Output SGST 4,590, Output IGST 6,480

slides.narration: To post the sales book, each customer is debited with the invoice total. Sales account is credited with the net total of rupees one lakh thirty thousand five hundred. The output tax accounts are credited with the tax collected. The debits and credits both total rupees one lakh forty six thousand one hundred sixty. A credit sale of an old asset would not come here but to the journal proper.

slides.heading: Quick check: document and book
slides.body_md: Match each source document with its book.
slides.narration: Think about who issues each document and what has happened to the goods. A bill for goods bought, a bill for goods sold, and the two notes for goods sent back or received back each have their own book.

slides.heading: Returns: debit notes and credit notes

rows: The seller, who takes goods back

visual.alt: Table comparing a debit note and a credit note: who issues each, to whom, what it says and the book in which it is recorded

slides.narration: When goods are returned, the buyer sends the supplier a debit note, which says the supplier is debited. The return is recorded in the purchases return book. When a seller takes goods back, he sends the customer a credit note, which says the customer is credited. The return is recorded in the sales return book. Tax on the returned goods is reversed at the same rate.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the two returns books
slides.body_md: Anvi Traders: goods returned to **Kishore Suppliers** (debit note) and by **Lalit Agencies** (credit note).
bullets: Purchases return: net ₹5,400 + tax ₹648 = **₹6,048**.
Sales return: net ₹3,600 + tax ₹432 = **₹4,032**.

visual.alt: Returns books of Anvi Traders: debit note to Kishore Suppliers for 5,400 plus tax, total 6,048 rupees; credit note from Lalit Agencies for 3,600 plus tax, total 4,032 rupees

slides.narration: Anvi Traders returned goods to Kishore Suppliers. The net value was rupees five thousand four hundred, and with tax the debit note is rupees six thousand forty eight. Lalit Agencies returned goods to Anvi Traders, with net value rupees three thousand six hundred, and the credit note is rupees four thousand thirty two. The tax in each note is split equally between central and state tax.

slides.heading: Quick check: debit note
slides.body_md: Decide who issues the note and where it is recorded.
slides.narration: A firm returns defective goods to its supplier and sends a note. Decide whether that note is a debit note or a credit note, and then decide in which return book it is recorded.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: tax payable after returns
slides.body_md: Output tax on sales, less output tax on sales returns, **less** input tax on purchases net of returns.

visual.alt: Tax position of Anvi Traders for July after returns: CGST payable 678, SGST payable 678, IGST payable 3,240 rupees

slides.narration: After returns, Anvi Traders has central tax on sales of rupees four thousand three hundred seventy four and central input tax of rupees three thousand six hundred ninety six. So central tax payable is rupees six hundred seventy eight, and state tax payable is the same. Integrated tax on sales is rupees six thousand four hundred eighty against input of rupees three thousand two hundred forty, so rupees three thousand two hundred forty is payable. All rates are imagined.

slides.heading: Quick check: the debit note amount
slides.body_md: Find the total value of a debit note, including tax.
slides.narration: First find the net value of the goods returned, using the trade discount. Then add tax at the rate given. The total is the amount of the debit note.

slides.heading: The journal proper
slides.body_md: The book of original entry for everything that fits **no special book**.

rows: Assets Dr, to liabilities and Capital
Charity or Advertisement Dr, to Purchases
Loss by Fire Dr, to Purchases

visual.alt: Table of journal proper entries: opening entry, credit purchase of an asset, adjustment, rectification, transfer, goods for personal use, goods given away and goods lost by fire, each with an example and the entry

slides.narration: The journal proper is for entries that fit no special purpose book. These include the opening entry, the credit purchase or sale of an asset, adjustment entries, rectification entries and transfer entries. It also holds the entries for goods taken by the owner, goods given as charity or free samples, and goods lost by fire. In each of the last three, Purchases account is credited at cost.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: journal proper entries
slides.body_md: **Kavya Stores**, an imagined shop, April. Furniture on credit, with tax at an imagined 12%, then four entries that credit Purchases.

rows: *(Being furniture bought on credit from Raj Furnishers; tax at an imagined 12%)*
*(Being goods taken by the owner for personal use)*

visual.alt: Journal proper of Kavya Stores for April: furniture bought on credit for 50,400 rupees including tax, drawings 6,000, charity 3,500, free samples 2,000 and loss by fire 18,000

slides.narration: Kavya Stores bought furniture on credit for rupees forty five thousand plus tax of rupees five thousand four hundred, so the supplier is credited with rupees fifty thousand four hundred. The owner took goods of rupees six thousand, which is drawings. Goods of rupees three thousand five hundred went as charity, rupees two thousand as free samples, and rupees eighteen thousand were lost by fire. In each of these four, Purchases account is credited.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: the opening entry
slides.body_md: Assets are **debited**; liabilities and **Capital** are credited, with Capital as the balancing figure.

rows: *(Being the assets, liabilities and capital brought forward at the start of the year)*

visual.alt: Opening entry of Kavya Stores: assets of 2,35,000 rupees debited; creditors 35,000, bank loan 50,000 and capital 1,50,000 credited

slides.narration: At the start of the year, Kavya Stores has assets of rupees two lakh thirty five thousand and owes rupees eighty five thousand to outsiders. The opening entry debits each asset and credits each liability. Capital is the balancing figure, which is rupees one lakh fifty thousand. The two sides of the entry are equal, so the books begin with the accounting equation in balance.

slides.heading: Quick check: asset or goods?
slides.body_md: Decide which book records a credit sale of an old machine.
slides.narration: Think about what the sales book is meant to record. Is an old machine goods in which the firm deals, or an asset? Then decide whether the reason given explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: Purchases and sales books: credit transactions in goods, at the net amount.
Debit note to the supplier, credit note to the customer; tax is reversed at the same rate.
Totals are posted to the ledger.
Journal proper: opening, adjustment, rectification, transfer, drawings, charity, free samples, loss by fire.

rows: Credit transactions in goods only, at the net amount after trade discount; tax columns at the stated rate
Debit note to the supplier, credit note to the customer; tax is reversed at the same rate
Totals of each book are posted to the ledger; debits equal credits
Everything else: opening, rectification, adjustment, transfer, drawings, charity and loss

visual.alt: Summary table of the purchases, sales and returns books, posting and the journal proper

slides.narration: To sum up. The purchases and sales books record credit transactions in goods at the net amount after trade discount, with tax columns at the rate given. Returns go to the return books through debit notes and credit notes. Each book is totalled and posted to the ledger. All other entries go to the journal proper, and goods that leave the business without a sale are credited to Purchases.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Deduct trade discount first; compute tax on the net amount.
Same state: CGST and SGST in equal parts; another state: IGST.
Goods taken, given away or lost: credit Purchases at cost.
Always add a narration in brackets.

rows: Deduct trade discount before entering the amount
Only the net amount is recorded
Compute tax on the net amount at the rate given
Tax is not charged on the discount
Use IGST for another state, CGST and SGST for the same state
The two cases never mix on one invoice
Credit Purchases when goods leave without a sale
Drawings, charity and fire loss all use this rule

visual.alt: Exam tips table for the purchases, sales and returns books and the journal proper

slides.narration: In the examination, deduct the trade discount first and compute tax on the net amount at the rate given in the problem. Use central and state tax for the same state and integrated tax for another state. Whenever goods leave the business without a sale, credit Purchases at cost. And always write a short narration in brackets under each journal entry.

notes.title: Recording of Transactions II: Special Purpose Books — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Special purpose books
sections.body_md:
When transactions are many, recording all of them in one journal is slow and crowded. Books are therefore divided by kind of transaction. The advantages are **division of work**, **specialisation**, **saving of time** and **easy reference**.

The books are the cash book, the petty cash book, the purchases book, the sales book, the purchases return book and the sales return book. Entries that fit none of them go to the **journal proper**. Each book is totalled and posted to the ledger.

key_terms.definition_md: A book of original entry kept for one kind of transaction, such as cash or credit purchases.
The paper that proves a transaction, such as an invoice, a cash memo, a cheque, a voucher or a note.

sections.heading: 2. The cash book: simple and with a bank column
sections.body_md:
The **cash book** is a book of original entry and also the cash account of the ledger. **Receipts** go on the debit side and **payments** on the credit side.

A **simple cash book** has one amount column for cash. Its balance is a debit balance or nil, since a firm cannot pay out more cash than it holds. A **two-column cash book** has a cash column and a bank column on each side. Each column is totalled and balanced separately: the difference is written as Balance c/d on the smaller side and brought down as Balance b/d on the other.

key_terms.definition_md: A book in which cash and bank receipts and payments are entered; it is also the cash account.
A cash book with one amount column, for cash only.
A cash book with a cash column and a bank column on each side.

sections.heading: 3. Contra entries, cheques, bank charges and overdraft
sections.body_md:
A **contra entry** is a transaction between the cash column and the bank column. It is written once on each side of the cash book and marked **C**. Cash deposited into the bank: credit in the cash column, debit in the bank column. Cash withdrawn from the bank for office use: debit in the cash column, credit in the bank column.

A cheque received and deposited is a debit in the bank column. A payment by cheque and **bank charges** are credits in the bank column; interest credited by the bank is a debit. A **bank overdraft** is a credit balance in the bank column: it is carried down on the debit side and brought down on the credit side.

key_terms.definition_md: An entry affecting both the cash and the bank column, shown on both sides of the cash book and marked C.
The amount by which the firm has paid out more than its bank balance, shown as a credit balance in the bank column.
The fees charged by the bank, recorded as a payment in the bank column.

sections.heading: 4. Petty cash book and the imprest system
sections.body_md:
Small expenses such as stamps, fares and tea are paid by a **petty cashier**. Under the **imprest system** the head cashier gives a fixed sum, the **imprest**, and at the end of the period reimburses exactly the amount spent, so the fixed sum is restored.

An **analytical petty cash book** has a receipts column, a total payments column and analysis columns for postage, stationery, conveyance, cartage and sundries. The analysis columns add up to the total column. The balance is carried down, and the reimbursement added: balance plus reimbursement equals the imprest.

key_terms.definition_md: The fixed sum advanced to the petty cashier; the amount spent is reimbursed so that it is restored.
A book in which small payments are recorded by the petty cashier.
A petty cash book with columns that classify each payment under heads.

sections.heading: 5. Purchases and sales books: trade discount and tax
sections.body_md:
The **purchases book** records credit purchases of goods; the **sales book** records credit sales of goods. Format: date, invoice number, name of supplier or customer, L.F., amount. Only the **net amount** after trade discount is entered; trade discount is not recorded separately. Cash purchases and sales go to the cash book; assets bought or sold on credit go to the journal proper.

**As of 2024.** With goods and services tax, tax columns are added: CGST and SGST in equal parts for a supply within a state, IGST for a supply between states. Tax is computed on the net amount at the rate stated in the problem (all rates in this chapter are imagined). Tax on purchases is debited to Input CGST, SGST or IGST accounts; tax on sales is credited to Output accounts.

**Posting:** purchases book: Purchases and Input tax accounts debited, suppliers credited. Sales book: customers debited, Sales and Output tax accounts credited.

sections.heading: 6. Returns books and the journal proper
sections.body_md:
Goods returned to a supplier are recorded in the **purchases return book** (return outwards) from a **debit note** issued by the buyer. Goods returned by a customer are recorded in the **sales return book** (return inwards) from a **credit note** issued by the seller. Tax on the returned goods is reversed at the same rate.

The **journal proper** holds entries that fit no special book: the **opening entry** (assets debited; liabilities and capital credited), **credit purchase or sale of an asset**, **adjustment**, **rectification** and **transfer** entries, and entries for goods taken by the owner (**Drawings Dr, Purchases Cr**), given as charity or free samples (**Charity or Advertisement Dr, Purchases Cr**) or lost by fire (**Loss by Fire Dr, Purchases Cr**). Each entry has a narration in brackets.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of an imagined trading firm proposes to keep separate books for cash, purchases, sales and returns instead of one journal for every transaction. The main reason is that separate books

options.text_md: make the ledger unnecessary
let the work be divided among several staff, make each clerk a specialist and allow quick reference to one kind of transaction
remove the need for a trial balance
ensure that no clerical error can ever occur

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** let the work be divided among several staff, make each clerk a specialist and allow quick reference to one kind of transaction. Dividing the work among clerks, specialising each book and saving time are the gains. These books do not replace the ledger or the trial balance, and they cannot guarantee freedom from error.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the cash book of an imagined firm is correct?

options.text_md: It is a ledger account only and has no original entries
It records only credit transactions of the firm
It records only transactions in which no cash is involved
It is a book of original entry and also serves as the cash account of the ledger

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It is a book of original entry and also serves as the cash account of the ledger. Cash transactions are first entered in the cash book, and the book is balanced like the cash account, so no separate cash account is posted. It is not only a ledger and it deals with cash, not credit, transactions.

questions.stem_md: In a cash book, cash received from a customer for goods sold on the spot is entered on the

options.text_md: debit side, because it is a receipt
credit side, because it is a receipt
debit side, because it is a payment
credit side, because it is a payment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** debit side, because it is a receipt. Receipts are shown on the debit side and payments on the credit side. Cash received for goods is therefore a debit entry, and it is not a payment.

questions.stem_md: While balancing the cash column of Mohit Gadgets, an imagined shop, the clerk finds that payments exceed receipts including the opening balance. This indicates

options.text_md: a bank overdraft
a credit balance to be carried down in the cash column
a mistake, because the cash in hand can never be a negative balance
a profit for the month

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a mistake, because the cash in hand can never be a negative balance. A firm cannot pay out more cash than it holds, so the cash column always has a debit balance or nil. Payments above receipts mean an entry is wrong or missing. An overdraft belongs to the bank column, and a cash shortfall is not profit.

questions.stem_md: In a two-column cash book a contra entry is one in which

options.text_md: a debtor is credited and the bank column is debited
only the bank column is affected
both the cash column and the bank column are affected, so the entry appears on both sides of the same book
a nominal account is debited and a personal account is credited

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** both the cash column and the bank column are affected, so the entry appears on both sides of the same book. A contra entry moves money between cash and bank, so it needs a line on each side of the cash book and is marked C. The other descriptions involve accounts that appear in the ledger as well.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following transactions of Tanvi Boutique, an imagined shop, is a contra entry?

options.text_md: Cash of ₹15,000 deposited into the bank
Rent of ₹6,000 paid by cheque
Cash sales of ₹9,000
A cheque of ₹20,000 received from a customer and deposited

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Cash of ₹15,000 deposited into the bank. Only the deposit of cash into the bank is an exchange between the cash and bank columns. Rent and cash sales affect one column and a nominal account, and a customer cheque affects the bank column and a personal account.

questions.stem_md: At the end of November the bank column of Vikram Plastics, an imagined firm, shows a credit balance of ₹9,500. This means

options.text_md: the bank owes the firm ₹9,500
the firm holds ₹9,500 in cash
cheques of ₹9,500 are yet to be deposited
the firm has overdrawn its bank account by ₹9,500

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the firm has overdrawn its bank account by ₹9,500. A credit balance in the bank column means the firm has paid out more than it deposited, so the bank has lent the difference as an overdraft. A favourable balance would be a debit balance.

questions.stem_md: On 14 March 2027 Nisha Footwear, an imagined shop, received a cheque for ₹18,000 from a customer, Ajay Rao, and deposited it in the bank the same day. In the two-column cash book the entry is

options.text_md: a debit in the cash column, To Ajay Rao
a debit in the bank column, To Ajay Rao
a credit in the bank column, By Ajay Rao
a credit in the cash column, By Ajay Rao

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a debit in the bank column, To Ajay Rao. A cheque deposited at once increases the bank balance, so the bank column is debited and the customer is credited in the ledger. The cash column is not touched, and a receipt is never entered on the credit side.

questions.stem_md: The bank charged ₹450 as service charges on the current account of Omkar Stores, an imagined shop, and the firm learnt of it from the bank statement. In the two-column cash book the entry is made

options.text_md: on the credit side, By Bank charges, in the bank column
on the debit side, To Bank charges, in the bank column
on the credit side, By Bank charges, in the cash column
on the debit side, To Bank charges, in the cash column

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** on the credit side, By Bank charges, in the bank column. Bank charges reduce the bank balance, so they are a payment in the bank column. No cash moves, so the cash column is untouched.

questions.stem_md: Under the imprest system of petty cash, the head cashier

options.text_md: gives the petty cashier a different sum every week
gives the petty cashier a fixed sum and later reimburses exactly the amount spent
pays all small expenses directly and keeps no petty cash
takes back the whole balance each week and gives nothing in return

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** gives the petty cashier a fixed sum and later reimburses exactly the amount spent. The imprest is a fixed float. At the end of the period the amount spent is reimbursed so that the float is restored. The other options do not describe a fixed advance that is topped up.

questions.stem_md: The imprest of Sheetal Bookshop, an imagined shop, is ₹4,000. In the week the petty cashier paid ₹240 on postage, ₹860 on stationery, ₹410 on conveyance, ₹780 on cartage and ₹390 on sundries. The amount to be reimbursed is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹2,680. The reimbursement equals the amount spent: 240 + 860 + 410 + 780 + 390 = ₹2,680. ₹1,320 is the balance still in hand, ₹4,000 is the imprest itself, and the last option adds two unrelated figures.

questions.stem_md: What distinguishes an analytical petty cash book from a plain one?

options.text_md: It is kept by the head cashier and not by the petty cashier
It records only receipts
It is never balanced
Extra columns that classify each payment under heads such as postage and stationery

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Extra columns that classify each payment under heads such as postage and stationery. The analysis columns split each payment by head, so each head total can be posted once. It is kept by the petty cashier, records payments as well as receipts, and is balanced each period.

questions.stem_md: The imprest of an imagined office is ₹3,000. At the start of a week the petty cashier already has ₹750 in hand. To bring the float to the imprest, the head cashier gives
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹2,250. The float must equal the imprest, so the head cashier gives 3,000 − 750 = ₹2,250. ₹750 is what is already there, ₹3,000 would push the float above the fixed amount, and ₹3,750 would exceed it even more.

questions.stem_md: Esha Tailors, an imagined shop, withdrew ₹7,000 from its bank for use in the office. In the two-column cash book this is entered

options.text_md: as a debit in the bank column and a credit in the cash column, marked C
as a debit in the cash column only
as a debit in the cash column and a credit in the bank column, marked C
as a credit in the bank column only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** as a debit in the cash column and a credit in the bank column, marked C. Cash comes in (debit in the cash column) and the bank balance falls (credit in the bank column); the two lines together are a contra entry. The second option is a deposit, and the last two leave out one of the two equal lines.

**Assertion (A):** The cash book is a book of original entry.

**Reason (R):** The cash book is balanced at the end of the period in the same way as a ledger account.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true. But being balanced like a ledger account is why the cash book also serves as the cash account; it does not explain why it is a book of original entry, which is because transactions are first recorded in it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The cash column of a cash book can never show a credit balance.

**Reason (R):** A firm cannot pay out more cash than it has received or holds.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R is the reason for A: payments are limited by the cash available, so the debit side, with the opening balance, is always at least as large as the credit side.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Cash deposited into the bank is entered only in the bank column of the cash book.

**Reason (R):** The cash column and the bank column are two parts of the same cash book.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: a deposit is entered twice, as a credit in the cash column and a debit in the bank column (a contra entry). R is true, since both columns belong to one book, and that is why one book can show both lines.

questions.stem_md: A bank overdraft is shown in the bank column of the cash book as a debit balance.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** An overdraft is a credit balance in the bank column: the firm has paid out more than it deposited. It is carried down on the debit side, and the next period begins with it on the credit side.

questions.stem_md: On the imprest system, the sum reimbursed at the end of a period equals the total payments made by the petty cashier in that period.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Reimbursing exactly what was spent restores the float to the fixed amount, so the petty cashier starts the next period with the imprest again.

questions.stem_md: The cash column of the cash book always has a ___ balance or nil, but the bank column may show a ___ balance when the firm has an overdraft.
questions.solution_md: Cash can only be a debit balance or nil, since payments cannot exceed cash held; an overdraft is a credit balance in the bank column.

questions.stem_md: Under the ___ system the petty cashier receives a fixed sum, and at the end of the period the amount ___ is paid to him by the head cashier.
questions.solution_md: The imprest system gives a fixed float; the amount spent is reimbursed so the float is restored.

options.text_md: Write the equal total on both sides and bring the balance down as Balance b/d on the other side

questions.stem_md: Give any two advantages of keeping special purpose books instead of recording every transaction in one journal.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: Why is the cash book called both a book of original entry and a ledger?

answer.model_answer_md: Cash receipts and payments are **first entered** in the cash book, so it is a book of original entry. It is **balanced** like an account, receipts on the debit side and payments on the credit side, so it serves as the cash account and none is kept in the ledger.

a gain of the buyer shown in the profit and loss account
a discount recorded in a separate column of the cash book
a reduction in the list price given by the seller, so it is not recorded separately in the books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a reduction in the list price given by the seller, so it is not recorded separately in the books. a credit note, recorded in the sales return book
an invoice, recorded in the sales book

questions.solution_md: Reason, six books with their contents, and the journal proper.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Why kept:** one journal for everything would be slow and crowded; separate books give division of work, specialisation, saving of time and easy reference.

**The books:** (1) cash book: cash and bank receipts and payments, and it also serves as the cash account; (2) petty cash book: small payments on the imprest system; (3) purchases book: credit purchases of goods; (4) sales book: credit sales of goods; (5) purchases return book: goods returned to suppliers, from debit notes; (6) sales return book: goods returned by customers, from credit notes.

Entries that fit none of these are recorded in the **journal proper**.
